concepts.heading: Perpetual vs Solvable Problems
concepts.alt: A guide holding a pie chart with one large slice and one small slice
concepts.plain: About 7 in 10 relationship problems never fully go away.

concepts.heading: What Makes a Problem Perpetual?
concepts.alt: Two guides standing back to back, one holding a sun and one holding a moon, both smiling
concepts.plain: Some problems come from who you each are. They keep coming back.

concepts.heading: Solvable Problems
concepts.alt: A guide fitting the last piece into a small jigsaw puzzle
concepts.plain: Other problems are about one situation and can be fixed with a good talk.

concepts.heading: The Paradigm Shift
concepts.plain: Good communication will not solve everything. The goal is to live well with differences.

concepts.heading: When Perpetual Problems Become Gridlocked
concepts.alt: On opposite sides of a locked gate, arms crossed
concepts.plain: A problem is gridlocked when you cannot talk about it without getting hurt or angry.

concepts.heading: Dreams Within Conflict
concepts.alt: A guide looking up at a thought bubble that holds a small glowing star
concepts.plain: Under a stuck fight there is usually a hope or dream. Ask about it.

concepts.heading: Perpetual Problems in Different Relationships
concepts.plain: Every kind of relationship has differences that keep coming back.

checks.prompt: What share of relationship problems are perpetual?
checks.explanation: 69%. Gottman found that 69% of relationship problems are perpetual, meaning they never fully go away.

options: When partners can't discuss it without hostility, hurt or shutdown
checks.explanation: When partners can't discuss it without hostility, hurt or shutdown. A perpetual problem becomes gridlocked when partners can no longer discuss it without hostility, hurt, or shutdown.

35b644bf-cdeb-433a-b4ed-36d3e8b7b691.takeaway: Most relationship problems never fully go away. The skill is talking about them kindly.

concepts.heading: Physiological Flooding & Self-Soothing
concepts.alt: A guide with a pounding heart on his chest and steam rising from his head
concepts.plain: Flooding is when a fight overwhelms your body and you cannot think.

concepts.heading: What Happens in Your Body
concepts.alt: A guide with a hand on her chest, a heartbeat line and a small alarm bell beside her
concepts.plain: Your heart races and your body goes into survival mode.

concepts.heading: Why You Can't Argue When Flooded
concepts.plain: In that state your brain cannot listen, care or solve problems.

concepts.heading: Recognizing the Signs
concepts.alt: A guide noticing her own clenched fist and slowly opening it
concepts.plain: Learn your own warning signs, like a tight chest or wanting to run.

concepts.heading: The 20-Minute Rule
concepts.alt: A guide holding a large kitchen timer
concepts.plain: Your body needs at least 20 minutes to settle down.

concepts.heading: How to Take a Break Without Stonewalling
concepts.alt: A making a time-out sign with her hands while B nods calmly
concepts.plain: Say you need a break and say when you will come back. That is not shutting down.

concepts.heading: Self-Soothing Techniques
concepts.alt: A guide breathing slowly with eyes closed, one hand on her belly
concepts.plain: Use the break to calm your body: slow breathing, a walk, music.

concepts.heading: Flooding in Your Relationships
concepts.plain: Any heated talk can flood you. Agree on a pause signal ahead of time.

checks.prompt: How long does the body need to return to baseline after flooding?
checks.explanation: At least 20 minutes. Gottman's research shows the body needs at least 20 minutes to return to physiological baseline after flooding.

checks.after: How to Take a Break Without Stonewalling
checks.prompt: What makes a break different from stonewalling?
options: Saying so and committing to return
checks.explanation: Saying so and committing to return. The difference between a healthy break and stonewalling is communication and a commitment to return.

079ab209-42bc-4ab4-bd65-cfb6010b50f3.takeaway: When your heart is racing you cannot argue well. Take 20 minutes, calm down, then come back.

concepts.heading: Repair Attempts: The Secret Weapon
concepts.alt: A guide holding a small toolbox with a heart on it
concepts.plain: Repair attempts are the biggest sign of whether a relationship will last.

concepts.heading: What Is a Repair Attempt?
concepts.alt: Two guides in the middle of an argument, B offering a small white flag with a sheepish smile
concepts.plain: A repair attempt is anything that lowers the tension, like a joke, a touch or "sorry".

concepts.heading: Why Repair Attempts Matter More Than Conflict Style
concepts.plain: How often you fight matters less than whether your repairs work.

concepts.heading: Why Repairs Sometimes Fail
concepts.alt: A guide holding out an olive branch toward a small raincloud
concepts.plain: Repairs only land when there is enough goodwill between you.

concepts.heading: Making Repairs More Effective
concepts.plain: Try early, mean it, and notice when your partner is trying.

concepts.heading: Building a Repair-Friendly Relationship
concepts.alt: Relaxed on a sofa, writing a short list together
concepts.plain: Talk in calm times about what helps each of you reconnect.

concepts.heading: Repair Attempts in Your Relationships
concepts.plain: Repair works in every relationship. Use it early.

concepts.heading: After the Fight: Processing It Together
concepts.plain: Once you are both calm, talk through the fight in five steps: feelings, both views, triggers, your part, a plan.

options: Any effort to reduce tension during conflict
checks.explanation: Any effort to reduce tension during conflict. A repair attempt is any effort to reduce tension during conflict.

checks.after: Why Repair Attempts Matter More Than Conflict Style
checks.prompt: What predicts relationship success, according to Gottman?
checks.explanation: The success of repair attempts. Gottman found that the success of repair attempts — not conflict frequency or intensity — predicts relationship outcomes.

3ee9b0cb-166b-4569-9f48-738b9dcbf1ff.takeaway: A small move to ease tension mid-fight, like a joke or "I'm sorry", is what saves relationships.

concepts.heading: Conflict as Growth
concepts.alt: Two guides climbing a small hill together, helping each other up
concepts.plain: Conflict can bring you closer if you handle it with care.

concepts.heading: Softened Startup
concepts.alt: A guide starting a conversation with an open palm and a soft round empty speech bubble
concepts.plain: How a talk starts is almost always how it ends. Start softly.

concepts.heading: Complaint vs. Criticism
concepts.alt: A guide pointing calmly at a wristwatch
concepts.plain: A complaint is about what happened. Criticism attacks who the person is.

concepts.heading: Active Listening During Conflict
concepts.alt: A speaking while B listens closely, hand cupped to his ear
concepts.plain: Repeat back what you heard before you answer.

concepts.heading: Accepting Influence
concepts.alt: Each holding one side of a steering wheel, steering together
concepts.plain: Let your partner change your mind sometimes. Those relationships last.

concepts.heading: When Conflict Becomes Harmful
concepts.plain: Disagreement is normal. Fear, threats or control are not. That is harm.

concepts.heading: Seeking Professional Support
concepts.plain: Trained couples therapists can help.

checks.prompt: How a conversation begins predicts how it ends how often?
checks.explanation: 96% of the time. How a conversation begins predicts how it will end 96% of the time (Gottman).

checks.prompt: "I was upset that you were late to dinner" is a…
checks.explanation: Complaint about a specific behaviour. A complaint addresses a specific behavior: "I was upset that you were late to dinner."

2ef35e07-6674-474d-8049-a0b32d811819.takeaway: Start gently, complain about the behaviour and not the person, and let your partner influence you.
